lec05kp02-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp02-u01-p1-title.text: Two-layer network: two hidden units each ask a yes-or-no question; the output unit combines them

lec05kp02-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP01 ended with two parallel lines enclosing a strip that holds exactly the A points of XOR. How do we turn that into a network?

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p1|Wiring: inputs x1, x2 feed hidden unit 1 (g1 = x1 + x2 - 0.5, bit y1) and hidden unit 2 (g2 = x1 + x2 - 1.5, bit y2), which feed the output unit g_out = y1 - y2 - 0.5.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-4.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p1#4
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-4.text: Wiring of the two-layer network: inputs, hidden layer, output layer

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-38.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p1#38
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-38.text: Inputs only supply coordinates, not a layer: hidden + output = two layers

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-39.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p1#39
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-39.text: Each unit computes a score; its boundary is a line in the plane

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-42.name: term:Hidden layer
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-42.text:
Hidden layer: the row of units that
asks the small questions; each unit's
boundary is a line in the plane.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-43.name: term:Output layer
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-43.text:
Output layer: the unit that makes the
final classification from the codes.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-44.name: term:Two-layer network
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-44.text:
Two-layer network: hidden layer plus
output layer; the inputs do not count
as a layer.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-46.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p1#46
lec05kp02-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp02-p1-46.text:
Last KP's conclusion: two parallel
lines enclose a strip that holds
exactly the A points. Here it becomes
a network.

lec05kp02-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp02-u01-p2-title.text: Each line asks whether a point is on its positive side; the step rule records 1 if so, otherwise 0

lec05kp02-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p2-bridge.text: The two hidden units each ask a yes-or-no question. How does each unit turn a score into a bit?

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p2|Plane with the lines x1+x2 = 0.5 and 1.5, positive sides shaded with arrows; step rule y_j = 1 if g_j > 0 else 0.

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-4.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p2#4
lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-4.text: Each line has a positive side

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-30.name: fig:lec05-kp02-p2#30
lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-30.text:
Arrows point to the

colours overlap both

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-36.text: Step rule: positive side gives 1, otherwise 0

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-40.name: term:Step rule
lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-40.text:
Step rule: a positive score gives 1, otherwise 0 (a

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-41.name: term:Bit
lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-41.text: Bit: the 0 or 1 that the step rule gives.

lec05kp02-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp02-p2-43.text:
Every point gets two bits (y₁, y₂), one per

Hidden code: the two bits written together as [y₁,

steps.label: Two-layer net
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp02 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 11 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Wiring
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP02. Three prerequisites: score and positive side, the XOR and strip of KP01, and the step. One line cannot answer A or B, so first ask two yes-or-no questions with two lines: hidden unit 1 has the score g1 equal to x1 plus x2 minus 0.5 and hidden unit 2 has g2 equal to x1 plus x2 minus 1.5. Each unit outputs one bit, y1 and y2, which feed one output unit whose score is y1 minus y2 minus 0.5. The hidden layer is the row of units that asks the small questions; the output layer is the unit that classifies the codes; hidden plus output is a two-layer network, and the inputs only supply coordinates and are not a layer. Next, the next page covers the step rule.

steps.label: Step rule
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the wiring of the two-layer network. This page defines the step rule. For each line gj, a point on the positive side, that is with score above 0, gets 1 and otherwise 0, and exactly 0 also gives 0. The resulting 0 or 1 is a bit. The left plot is one plane with the lines x1 plus x2 equal to 0.5 and 1.5; the positive side of each is shaded and marked by an arrow, and where the colours overlap both lines are positive. Every point gets two bits, y1 and y2. Next, the next page covers walking (0, 1) through.

steps.label: One point
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the step rule. This page walks the point (0, 1) through. Into the first line: g1 equals 0 plus 1 minus 0.5 equal to 0.5, above 0, so y1 equals 1. Into the second line: g2 equals 0 plus 1 minus 1.5 equal to minus 0.5, at most 0, so y2 equals 0. The two bits written together, y equal to (1, 0), form the hidden code, like two position labels attached to the point. The flow reads top to bottom: input, two scores, step rule, hidden code (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the codes of the four points.

steps.label: Four codes
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on walking (0, 1) through. This page computes the scores and codes of the four points. (0, 0): g1 is minus 0.5 and g2 is minus 1.5, code (0, 0), class B. (0, 1) and (1, 0): g1 is 0.5 and g2 is minus 0.5, code (1, 0) for both, class A. (1, 1): g1 is 1.5 and g2 is 0.5, code (1, 1), class B. The two lines cut the plane into three bands with codes (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), and both A points are in the middle band (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the hidden space.

steps.label: Hidden space
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the codes of the four points. This page replaces every point by its code (y1, y2) and draws it in a new plane, the hidden space. (0, 0) is B, (1, 0) is A and is where two inputs merged, (1, 1) is B; nothing lands on (0, 1), so it is drawn hollow. The output score is g_out equal to y1 minus y2 minus 0.5. Setting it to 0 and rearranging gives y2 equal to y1 minus 0.5, a line in the hidden space. g_out above 0 is equivalent to y2 below y1 minus 0.5, that is, below the line, called A. Merging the two A points is harmless because they are the same class. Next, the next page covers checking the output scores.

steps.label: Check scores
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the hidden space. This page checks the output layer point by point. (0, 0): 0 minus 0 minus 0.5 equals minus 0.5, called B. (1, 0): 1 minus 0 minus 0.5 equals 0.5, called A, the position of the two A inputs. (1, 1): 1 minus 1 minus 0.5 equals minus 0.5, called B. The predictions of the four inputs are 0, 1, 1, 0 (A as 1, B as 0), exactly XOR, all four right. This only checks these four points and is not accuracy on new data (computed by program). Next, the next page covers back in the original plane.

steps.label: Original plane
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on checking the output scores. This page translates the network back to the original plane. y1 equal to 1 means x1 plus x2 above 0.5; y2 equal to 0 means x1 plus x2 at most 1.5. An output score above 0 is equivalent to the code being exactly (1, 0). So the whole network selects the strip 0.5 below x1 plus x2 at most 1.5, which is the strip of KP01: the hidden layer makes two judgments and the output layer says both hold. Check: the two A points have x1 plus x2 equal to 1, inside the strip, and the two B points have 0 and 2, outside (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the consequence of merging.

steps.label: Merging
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on back in the original plane. This page looks at the consequence of merging. In this example the two A points merge into code (1, 0), the output layer calls it A, and both are right. A common myth is that any merge is harmless. If points of different classes get the same code, called a code conflict, the output layer sees only the code and one code gets one verdict, so A or B is wrong and no later line can repair it. The right panel is a schematic, not this example. Note also that y1 and y2 are only on-the-positive-side bits, not class probabilities; this construction only shows that XOR can be represented, and for other tasks one must first check that the output layer can separate the hidden codes. Next, the next page covers exercise 1.

steps.label: Extension: Task 1
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the consequence of merging. This is the first exercise. Keep the hidden codes and change the output score to g_out equal to y1 minus y2 plus 0.5; what are the four predictions? Solution: the formula is as above; substituting the three positions gives 0.5 at (0, 0), 1.5 at (1, 0) and 0.5 at (1, 1); all three scores are positive, so all four inputs are called A. Check: the XOR truth is B, A, A, B, so the two B points are called A, 2 wrong. The bias shifts the line to y2 equal to y1 plus 0.5, which no longer separates B from A (computed by program). Next, the next page covers exercise 2.

steps.label: Extension: Task 2
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on exercise 1. This is the second exercise: which different inputs are merged, and why does this merge cause no conflict? Solution: the merged inputs are (0, 1) and (1, 0), whose hidden codes are both (1, 0); both points are class A in XOR, merging same-class points is harmless, and the output layer just calls this code A. Check: with this output line the two B points (0, 0) and (1, 1) are also called A; the cause is that the bias shifts the line, not the merge (computed by program). Next, the next page covers removing the step.

steps.label: Extension: Step
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on exercise 2. This page shows that the step cannot be dropped. Without the step, y1 equals x1 plus x2 minus 0.5 and y2 equals x1 plus x2 minus 1.5; substituting into g_out equal to y1 minus y2 minus 0.5 gives (x1 plus x2 minus 0.5) minus (x1 plus x2 minus 1.5) minus 0.5, which equals 0.5 and does not depend on x, so every point is called A and XOR gets 2 points wrong. A combination of linear forms is still linear, and the nonlinearity comes from the step (computed by program). This derivation is supplementary. That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
